cards.explanation: The phrase is "a stream of words." Zophar asks, "Should this stream of words go unanswered and such a speaker be vindicated?" (Job 11:2). He's talking about Job's speech, and he treats it like a faucet somebody forgot to turn off. I think Zophar has been holding this one in for a while.

The answer is False. Zophar calls Job's words "babbling" and asks, "Will you scoff without rebuke?" (Job 11:3). Those are not words you use for calm and humble. I think if Zophar had a gentle side, it stayed home that day.

The word is pure. Zophar says, "You have said, ‘My doctrine is sound, and I am pure in Your sight.’" (Job 11:4). He's putting Job's claim right out on the counter for everyone to look at. Whether he's quoting Job exactly is something I'll leave alone, because the text just says Zophar says it.

The answer is less than his iniquity deserves. Zophar says, "Know then that God exacts from you less than your iniquity deserves." (Job 11:6). Iniquity means wrongdoing. Zophar is saying Job is getting off easy, and I think Job did not enjoy hearing that one bit.

Zophar's point is that Job can't reach those deep things. He says they are "…higher than the heavens…" and "…deeper than Sheol…" and then asks, "…what can you do?" and "…what can you know?" (Job 11:8). He's using the questions to say Job can't reach them. That's a lot of mountain to climb with a stool and a dream.
The answer is True. Zophar asks, "If He comes along to imprison you, or convenes a court, who can stop Him?" (Job 11:10). The question answers itself. Nobody can stop Him.

The answer is that He takes note of it. Zophar says, "Surely He knows the deceit of men. If He sees iniquity, does He not take note?" (Job 11:11). It's another question where the answer is built in. Zophar says He takes note.

Zophar's point is that the witless man can't become wise. He says, "…a witless man can no more become wise than the colt of a wild donkey can be born a man!" (Job 11:12). A donkey colt is not getting born a man, and that's the picture. It's a sharp thing to say, and I think it's aimed at Job.

The answer is the iniquity in his hand. Zophar says, "…if you put away the iniquity in your hand…" (Job 11:14). It's one more step in his list of ifs. Put it down, and then the speech moves on to what comes after.

The answer is True. Zophar says, "…then indeed you will lift up your face without blemish; you will stand firm and unafraid." (Job 11:15). Both pieces are in the same verse. It's a nice picture, even with the sharp talk before it.

The picture says Job's misery will pass and be gone. Zophar says, "…you will forget your misery, recalling it only as waters gone by." (Job 11:16). Water that's gone by doesn't come back around. I think that's the picture he wants Job to see.
The answer is False. Zophar says, "…you will look around and lie down in safety." (Job 11:18). He never says Job will go without rest. In fact he says Job will be secure.
The word is court. Zophar says, "You will lie down without fear, and many will court your favor." (Job 11:19). To court someone's favor is to go looking for it. I bet that's a lot of attention.

The answer is their last breath. Zophar says, "But the eyes of the wicked will fail, and escape will elude them; they will hope for their last breath." (Job 11:20). It's a heavy way to end, and I think it's meant to sit hard. Zophar is putting it right beside his picture of a bright future.
